summary: Purple willow is a shrub or small tree native to Europe, western Asia and northwestern Africa, where it grows in wetlands such as river floodplains and lake margins. Its flexible, evenly sized stems have long been harvested for basketry, while its early catkins provide nectar for insects. Unlike most willows, its narrow leaves are opposite or nearly opposite, and male and female flowers grow on separate plants.

summary: Eastern cottonwood is a large, fast-growing tree native across much of North America. It establishes best on bare, sunny soil, so freshly exposed river mud after floods provides ideal seedbeds. Female trees release vast numbers of seeds on cotton-like strands, while established trees can also resprout after cutting and sometimes form clonal stands. Its soft wood is used for plywood and the interior parts of furniture.

Bearberry is a low evergreen shrub widespread around northern parts of the Northern Hemisphere, with southern populations confined to high elevations. Its trailing stems root at intervals and can form dense ground cover. White-to-pink urn-shaped flowers are followed by red fruits that may persist into early winter and are eaten by bears and other animals. The plant tolerates fire and may maintain a buried seed bank.

summary: Pepino is an evergreen South American shrub grown for its sweet fruit, whose flavour has been compared with honeydew and cucumber. It was already cultivated on the Peruvian coast when early Spanish chroniclers described it, and it appeared frequently in Moche art. The crop is usually propagated from cuttings and can set fruit without pollination, although pollination encourages fruiting. Its delicate fruit is sensitive to handling and travels poorly.

details.use: eaten fresh as a snack fruit

summary: Water mannagrass is a perennial wetland grass native to Europe, the Mediterranean region and western Asia. Its floating leaves trap a temporary film of gas that improves gas exchange and photosynthesis while submerged, helping the plant cope with floods. Before the nineteenth century its grain was widely gathered in Central Europe and Sweden and traded as far as England, although this use faded as wetlands disappeared and harvesting proved laborious.

summary: Euphorbia officinarum is a cactus-like shrub endemic to northern Africa. It grows in varied low- and middle-elevation terrain, from sea level to 1,900 metres, in arid conditions moderated by relatively high ocean-derived humidity. Its upright, star-sectioned stems carry strong paired spines and only tiny, reduced leaves. It flowers from summer into autumn, with fruit developing from late summer through autumn.

Tufted bulrush is a densely tufted perennial sedge with a northern and mountain distribution. It thrives in wet, acidic soils and peat, including bogs, moorland and wet heaths, and can persist after burning or heavy deer grazing. On flatter mountain mires it may grow with cottongrass; drainage can let it replace bog moss as the dominant plant. A 2016–2019 assessment classified it as endangered in mainland Portugal, where only three locations were recognized.

Eurasian thyme is a perennial herb of central and eastern Europe and Russia, growing in open dry meadows, grasslands and rocky places. In southern Banat, Serbia, its lemon-scented dried herb is made into tea, while fresh leaves flavour homemade jams and sweets. Studies of Hungarian populations found marked variation in their essential oils, identifying twelve chemical forms rather than one uniform composition.

details.use: used to flavour homemade jams, candies and similar confections

summary: Micropus supinus is a small annual flowering plant of the Mediterranean region that grows on basic substrates in very dry places. In mainland Portugal it is known from only a few scattered sites in the south and can be difficult to detect because its colonies are small and isolated. A 2016–2019 assessment classified it as vulnerable there, with agricultural intensification and urban expansion reducing its habitat.

Great brome is an annual Mediterranean grass introduced across much of the world. Its large spikelets carry long, rough, backward-barbed awns that readily catch like fish hooks. These sharp seeds can lodge in the paws or eyes of cats and dogs and penetrate sheep skin, while swallowed awns may injure a sheep's mouth or intestine. The grass is also a serious cereal weed because it competes with wheat and contaminates harvested seed.

summary: Grey field-speedwell is a sprawling, blue-flowered annual native to Europe, southwestern Asia, North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Korea and Japan. It has spread to many other countries, especially as a weed of cultivated ground. Its small flowers arise singly where leaf stalks meet the stem, and its two-lobed fruit capsules bear both long and short hairs, a useful distinction from similar speedwells.

Ivy fern is native to Macaronesia, northwestern Africa and mainland Portugal. It grows in humid woodland and other shaded places, including mossy walls, rock crevices and sheltered banks exposed to ocean moisture. In mainland Portugal, a 2016–2019 assessment found the population restricted to the Sintra mountains and Cape Roca and classified it as endangered as maintenance and rebuilding damaged its shaded wall and bank habitats.

Geranium reuteri is a large perennial herb endemic to the Canary Islands, where it grows in moist laurel woods, cloud forest and pine woodland. From a woody base it produces a rosette of deeply divided leaves and, from late March to mid-May, branched clusters of pink, five-petalled flowers. In suitable forest it can form brilliant carpets across the ground.

Singapore graveyard flower is a small tree native to the West Indies, southern Mexico, Belize and Guatemala. It is widely cultivated in warm regions for clusters of fragrant white flowers with yellow throats, set against glossy, blunt-tipped leaves. In Cambodia, the flowers are made into necklaces and used as offerings to deities, extending their role beyond ornament in gardens.
Sand couch-grass is a flowering grass represented in mainland Portugal by two native subspecies. One of these, Elymus farctus subsp. boreo-atlanticus, is also native to the Madeira archipelago.

Lemmon's marigold is a shrub native to southern Arizona and the northwestern Mexican states of Sonora and Sinaloa. It grows in woodland, cliffs and moist sites, producing many small flower heads in flat-topped clusters. In cultivation it can flower from autumn into spring, sometimes for as long as ten months. Its foliage releases a pungent scent when disturbed, and the plant tolerates drought in Mediterranean climates.
Sinapidendron gymnocalyx is a flowering plant in the cabbage family endemic to the Madeira archipelago.
Rumex thyrsoides is a flowering plant in the knotweed family native to mainland Portugal.

Umbrella papyrus is a grass-like sedge native to West Africa, Madagascar and the Arabian Peninsula. It is cultivated worldwide as an ornamental in gardens, pots, ponds and homes. The plant needs abundant moisture and can grow in shallow water, but it requires protection below 5°C. It can be propagated by dividing its roots or by placing a cut-off top upside down in water.

Hairy carpet weed is an annual herb native to Eurasia and Africa and introduced elsewhere. It grows from prostrate to somewhat upright stems covered in felt-like white hairs, with whorled leaves and tight clusters of small, petal-free flowers. The plant occurs on seasonally flooded land and has long served as both food and medicine across its broad native range; young leaves and stems are eaten as a vegetable in some tropical countries.

Fringed amaranth is a smooth annual herb found in North America and Mexico. It grows on sandy or gravelly slopes, in semidesert and in disturbed ground, usually flowering after summer rains in these dry regions. Plants can reach about 70 centimetres tall and bear greenish to maroon flowers. The species is considered an invasive weed.

Pink snowberry is a North American flowering shrub widespread from New Mexico through much of Mexico to Guatemala and Honduras. Its upright, branching growth can reach three metres, making it the tallest species in its genus. Small leaves are dark green above and paler beneath, while pink bell-shaped flowers are followed by white or pale pink fruits.
Calvary clover is a flowering member of the pea family found mainly around the western Mediterranean. It forms a partnership with the bacterium Sinorhizobium medicae, which can fix nitrogen.

False rye barley is a wild barley native to Europe, including Madeira, Crimea and the northern Caucasus, as well as northwestern Africa and the Levant; it has been introduced to Australia and New Zealand. It is an allotetraploid, meaning its chromosome sets came from ancestors carrying two different Hordeum genomes.
Cluster-leaf brightfig is a succulent species endemic to South Africa's Western Cape, where it forms part of the fynbos vegetation.
